newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Texas Instruments reports lower earnings.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Texas Instruments reports lower earnings.

text.p: Texas Instruments Inc. reported lower first-quarter earnings Tuesday but said semiconductor orders were growing again and pointed to strong demand for new chips as the market recovers from a dismal year in 1996.

The Dallas-based semiconductor giant said it had earnings of $129 million, or 66 cents a share, on revenues of $2.26 billion. A year earlier it earned $163 million, or 84 cents a share, on revenues of $2.67 billion.
The net results included a special pretax charge of $56 million primarily related to costs associated with the sale of the company's computer notebook business to Acer Group of Taiwan.

Texas Instruments said earnings from continuing operations rose to 70 cents per share from 68 cents and that first-quarter semiconductor orders grew at double-digit rates over the last three months of 1996.
The results were better than Wall Street analysts' expectations, but Texas Instruments stock, after rising initially, was off 25 cents at $82.75 in afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
While its first-quarter revenues from common memory chips were down from a year ago due to sharply lower prices, other semiconductor revenues were significantly higher.

The company said it saw rapid growth from so-called differentiated products such as digital signal processors, or DSPs, and mixed-signal/analog products, and that those products also showed higher operating profit margins.
Digital signal processors are chips that translate sounds and sight into digital form and are used in cellular phones, modems and digital video, among other products.

Chief Financial Officer Bill Aylesworth said the world semiconductor market should grow about 10 percent this year, following a decline of 9 percent in 1996. He said the digital signal processors business would continue to grow at around 35 percent per year.

Texas Instruments is the market leader in digital signal processor products and in recent months divested its defense-electronics business and notebook computer unit to concentrate on the specialized chips as well as mixed-signal/analog products.
Revenues from those products now account for more than 40 percent of the company's total semiconductor revenues.

"The opportunity we have today in DSPs is the biggest opportunity for TI since the invention of the integrated circuit," Chief Executive Officer Tom Engibous said in a statement. "This particular business has great potential to accelerate TI's move toward higher value, higher growth and better financial stability."

Aylesworth said Texas Instruments had seen some recent signs of improving price stability in the notoriously volatile memory chip market. Spot prices for 16-megabyte dynamic random access memory chips, which were below $6 in January, have since risen to between $9 and $10.
But Aylesworth cautioned that global oversupply was still a problem in spite of rapid growth in demand, and said it was premature to speculate if the recent price rise would continue.

It was an 80 percent collapse in DRAM, or dynamic random access memory chip, prices during 1996 that battered the global chip market, bringing Texas Instruments its first year of negative growth in over a decade.
